newsitem.title: USA: More than 70 arrested at Wall Street AIDS protest.
newsitem.headline: More than 70 arrested at Wall Street AIDS protest.

text.p: More than 70 AIDS activists were arrested on Monday at a Wall Street rally to protest the high price of AIDS drugs, police said.

More than 200 protesters marched through the Wall Street area early Monday morning, accompanied by police on foot and on motor scooters. The demonstration came on the 10th anniversary of a Wall Street rally by the AIDS activist group Act Up at the same site.
Some protesters threw fake blood at the New York Stock Exchange building, and the NYSE pulled down metal gates at several of its entrances.

Protesters were arrested for disorderly conduct as they sat down in the streets near the New York Stock Exchange, blocking Wall Street workers from going to their jobs. Others were arrested for crashing police barricades.
Police said one officer was injured and taken to the hospital. Details of the injury were not immediately available.

The protest brought the usually crawling pace of traffic to a virtual standstill as police were forced to block off several streets leading to the exchange. Workers were slowed on their way to their jobs as police checked for identification before letting them pass barricaded checkposts.
Louis Anemone, chief of department of the New York City police, said a total of about 250 police were out in force.
Act Up was protesting what it called "Wall Street greed." The protesters criticized big drug companies for overcharging AIDS patients.
"Drug companies are price gouging," said Kate Krauss, a spokeswoman for the group. "(Drug companies) make 20 percent profit, and people with AIDS have no choice but to pay these outrageous prices."
Act Up said the group chose the NYSE as its target because the exchange symbolizes the heart of corporate America.
Krauss said the group wanted drug companies to sharply lower their prices, and demanded that the Federal government and Congress investigate pricing.
Krauss said that 10 years ago the group had succeeded in getting at least one drug company to drop the price of AIDs drug AZT to about $6,500 from $10,000.
A U.S. pharmaceutical research group countered that the price of drugs to fight AIDs and the HIV virus were reasonable.

"A few years ago, AIDS activists were chanting, 'seven years, $2 billion dollars and, one lousy drug,'" said Jeff Trewhitt, a spokesman for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. "Today there are more than 42 approved medicines and 122 AIDS drugs in development."
The trade group said a cocktail of three medicines can reduce the amount of the HIV virus in a patient's body by up to 99 percent.
"This remarkable progress has not come cheaply," he said, citing the high costs of development.
He said the three-drug cocktail costs between $10,000 to $16,000 per year, a price that is cost effective, considering that hospital treatment is $100,000 a year or more.
An exchange spokesman said the market opened at the normal 9:30 a.m. EST (1430 GMT) time.
Protesters ended their demonstration in front of the exchange, where they chanted, "Fight AIDS, Act Up, Fight Back."
NYSE Chairman Richard Grasso came out of the exchange briefly around the time trading began.
"This is America," Grasso said. "People are free to speak their piece." Grasso conferred briefly with top police officials, then went back into the exchange building.
After the nearly three-hour protest, Act Up members said they were going to the police department's central booking unit as a "show of solidarity" with arrested protesters.
